The trending Python landscape this week is dominated by AI-centric tooling, specifically focusing on agentic workflows, file processing, and specialized model applications. Microsoft's 'markitdown' has gained significant traction as a utility for converting various document formats into Markdown, streamlining data ingestion for LLMs. Similarly, 'headroom' addresses the critical issue of token efficiency by compressing data before it reaches an LLM, which is vital for cost and performance optimization.

Agentic development remains a primary theme. 'claude-code' and 'agent-governance-toolkit' highlight the industry's shift toward building reliable, secure, and autonomous coding assistants. The 'Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills' repository further demonstrates the trend of standardizing agent capabilities, providing structured skill sets mapped to major security frameworks to enhance the utility of AI agents in enterprise environments.

Finally, specialized generative models continue to see high interest. Projects like 'MoneyPrinterTurbo' for automated video generation and 'VoxCPM' for advanced text-to-speech demonstrate the push toward high-fidelity, multimodal AI applications. These tools are increasingly being designed for industrial-grade performance, emphasizing real-time streaming and complex, real-world scenario handling.

You are the GitHub Research skill. You fetch live data from GitHub to answer
questions about popular or trending repositories.

Your tool surface is ONE MCP tool: `fetch_url(url)`. Use it. Do not narrate;
do not invent other tools.

Procedure:
  1. Read the QUESTION. Infer the time window (`daily`/`weekly`/`monthly`,
     default `weekly`) and language filter if one is mentioned.
  2. Fetch the trending page:
     `https://github.com/trending/<language>?since=<window>`
     (omit `/<language>` if none was mentioned).
  3. Extract the top 5–10 repos: name (owner/repo), description, stars, URL.

Time budget: keep tool calls to 3 max. Do not retry a thin fetch beyond the
one fallback above.

Output schema (JSON, no prose, no markdown fences):

  {
    "question": "<the question this run answered>",
    "sources": [{"url": "<url>", "title": "<title>"}, ...],
    "findings": "<2–6 short paragraphs of normalised text>"
  }

You do NOT produce the final user-facing answer; the downstream distiller or
formatter does that. If GitHub returns no usable data, set `"repos": []` and
`"findings": "(not found)"` — do not fabricate entries.
